questions.stem: Which structural component of an enveloped virus originates directly from the host cell's lipid membrane during the process of viral budding?

options.option_text: Capsid — the protein shell that directly encloses viral nucleic acid
Nucleocapsid — complex of viral RNA tightly coated with capsid proteins
Viral envelope — a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane
Tegument — a proteinaceous matrix layer situated beneath the viral envelope

questions.explanation: C is correct: enveloped viruses (e.g., Influenza, HIV, Herpes) acquire their outer lipid bilayer by budding through the host's plasma or nuclear membrane — the lipid composition is therefore host-derived, not virally encoded. A (Capsid) is wrong because the capsid is encoded by viral genes and assembled from viral proteins, not borrowed from the host. Tegument (D) is a virus-encoded proteinaceous layer unique to herpesviruses and is also not host-derived.

questions.stem: Viroids, the causative agents of diseases like Potato Spindle Tuber disease, differ from conventional viruses in one fundamental structural aspect — they:

options.option_text: Lack any protein coat (capsid) and consist entirely of naked circular ssRNA
Replicate only inside nuclei of animal cells by hijacking host DNA polymerase
Carry double-stranded DNA as their genetic material, unlike most plant pathogens
Are miniaturised conventional viruses with a reduced but structurally intact capsid

questions.explanation: A is correct: viroids are the smallest known plant pathogens — they are short (~250–400 nt) circular single-stranded RNA molecules with no protein coat whatsoever, distinguishing them from all conventional viruses. D is a common trap: viroids are not simply 'smaller viruses'; they genuinely lack any capsid. C is wrong because viroids carry RNA, not DNA. B is wrong because viroids infect only plants, not animals.

questions.stem: HIV belongs to the Retroviridae family. During HIV replication inside a host CD4⁺ T-cell, the enzyme reverse transcriptase performs which specific catalytic step?

options.option_text: Transcribes viral mRNA back into genomic double-stranded DNA in the host nucleus
Degrades host ribosomal RNA to preferentially redirect ribosomes toward viral proteins
Integrates the proviral DNA into host chromosomes using phosphodiester bond formation
Synthesises complementary DNA (cDNA) using the viral positive-sense ssRNA as template

questions.explanation: D is correct: reverse transcriptase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase — it reads the viral (+)ssRNA genome and produces a complementary DNA strand (cDNA), which is subsequently made double-stranded, giving dsDNA that is integrated into the host genome. C describes the function of integrase, a separate HIV enzyme, which is the most common distractor. A reverses the direction of transcription incorrectly. B describes a bacteriophage (T-phage) strategy, not HIV.

questions.stem: Prions are the infectious agents responsible for fatal spongiform encephalopathies such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) and Kuru. What single property fundamentally distinguishes prions from every other known class of pathogen?

options.option_text: They carry a short segment of non-coding RNA that accumulates in neuronal tissue
They consist solely of misfolded host-encoded proteins with absolutely no nucleic acid
They contain dsDNA but lack the capsid proteins typical of conventional DNA viruses
They survive only in primate hosts and are inactivated by standard autoclaving protocols

questions.explanation: B is correct: prions (PrPSc) are misfolded isoforms of a normal host brain protein (PrPC). They contain no DNA or RNA — they are the only known infectious agents that violate the central dogma (no nucleic acid required for replication). A is wrong and describes viroids, not prions. C is wrong because prions have no nucleic acid of any kind. D is wrong on two counts: prions can infect multiple mammalian species (e.g., BSE jumped from cattle to humans), and standard autoclaving does NOT reliably inactivate prions — they require prolonged high-temperature steam or NaOH treatment.

questions.stem: In a bacteriophage infection, the lysogenic cycle differs from the lytic cycle in that during lysogeny the phage:

options.option_text: Immediately expresses all structural genes, assembling new virions that lyse the host cell
Assembles capsid proteins in the cytoplasm well before any nucleic acid is injected into host
Integrates its genome into the host bacterial chromosome and replicates silently as a prophage
Degrades host ribosomes first so that all translation resources are redirected to phage proteins

questions.explanation: C is correct: in lysogeny, phage DNA (after circularisation) integrates into the host chromosome via phage-encoded integrase, becoming a prophage that is replicated passively with each round of host cell division. This can persist for many generations until an inducing signal (UV, chemicals) triggers excision and entry into the lytic cycle. A describes the lytic cycle, the most common distractor. D describes some lytic phages (e.g., T4 degrades host DNA) but is not characteristic of lysogeny. B is mechanistically incoherent — capsid assembly follows nucleic acid injection, not precedes it.

questions.stem: Type I interferons (IFN-α and IFN-β) are among the earliest antiviral defences of innate immunity. Their primary mechanism of protecting neighbouring uninfected cells involves:

options.option_text: They signal adjacent cells to express antiviral effector proteins such as 2-5A synthetase
They directly neutralise free viral particles extracellularly by acting as opsonins
They activate the classical complement cascade to immediately lyse virus-infected host cells
They stimulate B-lymphocytes to rapidly produce virus-specific neutralising IgM antibodies

questions.explanation: A is correct: IFN-α/β secreted by an infected cell bind IFNAR receptors on adjacent cells, triggering the JAK-STAT pathway, which induces an 'antiviral state' — upregulating interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) encoding effectors like 2-5A (oligoadenylate) synthetase (which activates RNaseL to degrade viral RNA), PKR (which phosphorylates eIF2α to halt translation), and Mx GTPases. This bystander protection is the canonical function. B describes opsonisation, a function of antibodies (IgG)/complement, not interferons. C (classical complement) requires antibody-antigen complexes and is an adaptive immune mechanism. D describes a function of T-helper cells and follicular dendritic cells, not interferons, and IgM production takes days — far slower than interferon action.

questions.stem: According to the Baltimore Classification System, a virus whose complete replication pathway follows the scheme — (+)ssRNA → dsDNA (via reverse transcriptase) → (+)ssRNA — belongs to which Baltimore group, and which well-known pathogen exemplifies it?

options.option_text: Group IV — Poliovirus, replicating via (+)ssRNA without involving any DNA intermediate
Group III — Reoviruses, replicating via dsRNA and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase only
Group VII — Hepadnaviruses (e.g., Hepatitis B), whose dsDNA genome uses an RNA intermediate
Group VI — Retroviruses (e.g., HIV), using reverse transcriptase to produce a dsDNA provirus

questions.explanation: D is correct: Baltimore Group VI are the retroviruses — their genome is (+)ssRNA, reverse transcriptase converts it to dsDNA (the provirus), which is then transcribed back to (+)ssRNA genomic copies and mRNAs. HIV is the classic example. The critical trap is Group VII (Hepadnaviruses — Hepatitis B virus), which also uses reverse transcriptase BUT their genome is partially dsDNA (not ssRNA), and the replication goes dsDNA → pregenomic RNA → dsDNA — the reverse of Group VI. A (Group IV, Poliovirus) uses no DNA intermediate at all — it replicates entirely via RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. B (Group III, Reoviruses) start with dsRNA and also use no DNA step. Examinees must distinguish Group VI (RNA genome → RT → DNA) from Group VII (DNA genome → RT → DNA) to answer correctly.
